title: Popcorn: Who doesn't love it?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with Speaker 3, who is Chuck's co-host segment voice) explore popcorn for Popcorn Day: what makes kernels pop (hull moisture between roughly 13 and 20 percent water), popcorn's American origins and archaeological evidence, early popping methods and the 1866 patented popper, the 1893 mobile popcorn machine, popcorn as cereal and flour, its role in movie theaters during the Depression and World War Two, the subliminal advertising hoax, the shift to yellow corn, TV-era popcorn, Percy Spencer and microwave popcorn, Orville Redenbacher, popcorn flavors and global varieties, popcorn packing material, industry size and theater markup, and clarified butter tips. The episode ends with listener mail about the show's listener-made music bumpers from Cecilia S.

segments.title: Opening and Popcorn Day
segments.summary: Hosts introduce Popcorn Day episode, credit listener Sean O'Shullman for the idea, and note popcorn is an American food.

segments.title: What popcorn is and why it pops
segments.summary: Popcorn is a variety of corn with a hard hull; moisture between about 13 and 20 percent inside the bran turns to steam that bursts the kernel. Rice and wheat do not pop because their hulls are porous.

segments.title: Early popcorn varieties and names
segments.summary: Andrew Smith's catalog of early popcorn varieties sold around 1901 to 1902, with names like Tom Thumb and Tattooed Yankee; popcorn was sold locally by the scoop or bag before branding.

segments.title: Home popping methods
segments.summary: Hosts describe their popping methods: stir-crazy style popper, air popping, a whirlypop stovetop popper, and the flavored popcorn salt and butter-flavored oil; Flavacol is used by movie theaters.

segments.title: Popcorn cultivation and regional production
segments.summary: Indigenous Americans farmed popcorn in South, Central and North America; farming moved to New England and later the Midwest, with Chicago becoming a hub. About 25 percent of US popped popcorn is grown in Nebraska, plus other states; Brazil and Argentina also grow a lot.

segments.title: Popcorn nutrition
segments.summary: Air-popped plain popcorn is low in calories and high in fiber and whole grain; toppings and oil change the nutrition. Fiber may be a concern for people with IBS.

segments.title: Ancient origins and early written accounts
segments.summary: Corn was domesticated from teosinte in Mexico about 9,000 years ago; popcorn is roughly 2,500 years old or more, with archaeological finds in South America. Sixteenth-century and seventeenth-century missionaries described popcorn use among the Aztecs and Peruvians.

segments.title: Pilgrims legend and transition
segments.summary: The legend that popcorn was served at the first Thanksgiving appears to be a nineteenth-century invention, around when popcorn became a favored American snack.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Nineteenth-century popcorn spread and early poppers
segments.summary: Popcorn seeds sold from the 1820s; Thoreau called popcorn a perfect winter flower; popcorn appeared in the 1848 Dictionary of Americanisms. Early popping over fires and on iron plates, then the first popcorn popper patent in 1866 with a wire mesh basket.

segments.title: Mobile popcorn machines and Cracker Jack
segments.summary: Charles Cretors patented a mobile popcorn machine in 1893, adapted from a peanut roaster, enabling sidewalk popcorn stands. Sweet popcorn appeared in the late nineteenth century, and Cracker Jack came along in 1896.

segments.title: Popcorn as cereal, flour, and pancakes
segments.summary: Ella Kellogg introduced popcorn pudding as a breakfast cereal at the Battle Creek Sanitarium, a predecessor to corn flakes and Corn Pops. Popcorn can also be ground into flour, used in gluten-free pancake mix and popcorn bread.

segments.title: Movie theaters and the Depression
segments.summary: Popcorn initially sold outside theaters; theater owners later brought vendors inside and began popping and selling it themselves because of the markup. R. J. McKenna lowered ticket prices during the Depression, relying on popcorn profits.

segments.title: World War Two sugar shortage and subliminal advertising hoax
segments.summary: Sugar shortages in World War Two pushed Americans toward salty popcorn, and in 1945 more than half of popcorn eaten was at theaters. James Vicary's subliminal advertising popcorn claim was a fabrication that he later admitted.

segments.title: Yellow corn, butter flavor, and television
segments.summary: Theaters switched to yellow corn which looked buttery; by 1990 about ten percent of commercial popcorn was white corn. Popcorn industry feared TV would hurt theater sales, but people popped popcorn at home while watching TV in the 1950s. Hosts discuss early disruption and technology fears.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Electric poppers and packaging innovations
segments.summary: Early electric poppers were fire hazards; Consumer Bulletin in the late 1960s tested popular models. TV Time packaging with sealed popcorn and separate seasoning compartments and Jiffy Pop are mentioned.

segments.title: Microwave popcorn and Percy Spencer
segments.summary: Percy Spencer at Raytheon, working with magnetrons, noticed a melted chocolate bar and tested popcorn; his 1946 microwave patent showed popcorn. Microwave popcorn came to the home in 1981.

segments.title: Orville Redenbacher and popcorn flavors
segments.summary: Orville Redenbacher and Charles Bowman bought a corn plant in Indiana in 1951, landed on the Red Bow variety, began selling branded popcorn in 1969, and sold the brand in 1976 to Hunt-Wesson Foods while he remained the face. US favorite flavors are salted, buttered, white cheddar, cheddar, and kettle.

segments.title: Eating popcorn, global flavors, and packing material
segments.summary: Hosts discuss eating habits and worldwide flavors such as yuzu salt and Kishu plum from a Japanese company. Popcorn used as packing material since the 1950s has issues with pests and grease; German researchers in 2021 made popcorn-based foam from scrap corn.

segments.title: Popcorn industry size, theater markup, and clarified butter
segments.summary: The US popcorn industry is about 850 million dollars, with bagged popcorn about 1.5 billion. Theater popcorn markup is about 1,275 percent (stated as 275 percent in transcript). Clarified butter or ghee avoids soggy popcorn.

segments.title: Wrap-up and book recommendation
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up popcorn and recommend Andrew Smith's book Pop Culture.

segments.title: Listener mail on music bumpers
segments.summary: Listener Cecilia S. praises the listener-made music bumpers and Jerry's song choices; hosts thank listeners and note the 12 to 16 second length limit.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts provide the email address for listener contact and the closing credits.
